bullets: The Trump administration’s “Trump Accounts” auto‑enroll every child born 2025‑2028 in a tax‑deferred savings account seeded with $1,000, expanding enrollment from under 8 million to over 70 million children overnight.

Rich donors like Michael Dell, Ray Dalio and SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell can now contribute overvalued individual stocks to groups of at least 5,000 kids, and families cannot refuse these stock gifts, despite the original law limiting investments to low‑risk index funds.

Legal experts warn the stock‑gift provision may violate the program’s congressional mandate, raising concerns about forced ownership of potentially controversial companies and lack of a mechanism for families to decline or “disclaim” such donations.

items.subject: 3 Years of Israel's Genocide in Gaza: By the Numbers
bullets: The newsletter presents a data-driven overview of three years of the Gaza conflict, detailing civilian casualty counts, displacement figures, and the scale of humanitarian aid delivered.
It highlights that over 30,000 Palestinians have been killed, more than 1.5 million displaced, and international aid has totaled roughly $10 billion since the conflict began.

items.subject: Is This Failed Actor Nepo Baby Now the Biggest Media Mogul Ever?
bullets: David Ellison’s 20‑year‑old film, costing $60 million, earned under 25% of its budget and a 34% Rotten Tomatoes rating, yet its failure financed a massive media consolidation led by his billionaire father’s investment.
Ellison, a nepo‑baby whose father is the world’s eighth‑richest, leveraged the flop’s fallout to become one of history’s largest media moguls, reshaping the industry.

The piece also claims CNN staff are overly optimistic about the network’s future under Ellison, questions Fox’s refusal to air Trump rallies, and condemns mainstream media’s coverage of the Gaza conflict.

items.subject: We Spoke to the Guy Who Snitched on Kimberly Guilfoyle (w/ Eric Deters)
bullets: Eric Deters, central to the WSJ expose, claims Kimberly Guilfoyle asked him for $100,000 to cover credit‑card debt before her Greek ambassadorship confirmation, promising access and favors in return.
Deters says he spent hundreds of thousands trying to influence Guilfoyle and Trump allies, was urged to connect with Tucker Carlson and ex‑IRS chief Billy Long, and now feels like a “dumbass.”

He alleges Jared Kushner’s firm received a $3 billion Saudi sovereign‑wealth investment (reports cite $2 billion) and that Dr. Abubakar Atiq Durrani performed 580 unnecessary surgeries, though total patient impact is unclear.

items.subject: Dems Warn Voters: Trump May Not Deliver Your Mailed-in Ballots
bullets: Democrats are now concerned that the Trump administration may undermine the safety of mailed ballots, citing new internal threats rather than foreign interference or fraud.

items.subject: These Democrats Are Good, Actually
bullets: Angie Nixon, though unlikely to win, is a strong Florida Senate candidate with charisma and smart campaigning, reflecting a broader trend of competent Democratic candidates across the cycle.
The author contrasts Democratic strength with Republican weakness, naming Susan Collins and Vivek Ramaswamy as the only notable GOP contenders while dismissing others as inept or uncommitted.
He warns Democrats to learn from this disparity, implying they must improve candidate quality and campaign strategy to stay competitive.

items.subject: EXCLUSIVE: Hear a New Poem From Acclaimed Palestinian Poet Mosab Abu Toha
bullets: Mosab Abu Toha, a Gaza-born poet, delivers a raw, personal poem that recounts the terror of Israeli airstrikes, the loss of family, and the ongoing suffering of Palestinians, citing specific incidents such as a 2008 F‑16 raid and the 2023‑24 civilian casualties in Jabalia and Khan Younis.

The piece frames the Palestinian experience as louder than any military noise, urging U.S. President Joe Biden to recognize the human tragedy, and highlights Abu Toha’s recent accolades: 2025 Pulitzer Prize for commentary, 2024 OPC Flora Lewis Award, and a 2023 National Book Critics Circle Award finalist nod.

items.subject: Republicans Have an Andrew Tate Eel-Sex Problem
bullets: Andrew and Tristan Tate face extradition to the UK on rape, assault, and trafficking charges, with new court filings revealing bestiality claims involving an eel and a horse, and allegations that Tate coerced a 17‑year‑old into producing porn for $1,000 a day.

High‑profile Republicans—including Tucker Carlson, Candace Owens, Benny Johnson, Alina Habba, Ric Grenell, Paul Ingrassia, and even Trump Jr.—have publicly defended or supported the Tates despite the escalating evidence of sexual crimes.

In Indiana, staffer Paul Tinkle was fired after making an “OK” hand sign, sparking a debate over alt‑right symbolism that drew support from Turning Point USA, Jack Posobiec, and the Blaze, while local GOP officials and the party leadership denied responsibility for his dismissal.

items.subject: Breaking The Wall
bullets: AI agents that can autonomously manage personal finances could trigger continuous deposit shifts, threatening banks' cheap funding and potentially creating agentic bank runs.

Crypto’s blockchain infrastructure is finally finding purpose as tokenized real‑world assets—equities, treasuries, commodities—are moving on‑chain, with Solana processing more trades than the NYSE in September and regulators granting exemptions for tokenized stock trading.
Investors should now focus on who will capture the economics of these on‑chain financial products as they gain regulatory approval and mainstream adoption.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Our Big Fat Greek Bribery Scandal
bullets: Kimberly Guilfoyle, appointed U.S. ambassador to Greece, allegedly asked Trump donor Eric Deters to wire $100,000 to her Amex card, promising access to senior officials in exchange, per text messages reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Guilfoyle’s texts show she offered to deliver favors from the Secretary of Defense, Treasury, IRS, and others, while Deters complained he’d paid $300,000 over years without receiving any promised assistance.

The piece frames the episode as another example of Trump‑era corruption, noting Trump earned over $2 billion from similar grifts last year, and suggests the scandal is unlikely to be the last before the midterms.

items.subject: ICE Jailed a Rabbi For Protesting Israel. Now He Can’t Observe His Faith
bullets: ICE detained 35‑year‑old anti‑Zionist Satmar rabbi Yehnotan Ovadia, who entered on a religious worker visa in 2022, throughout Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Sukkot, forcing him to pray beside a toilet and causing a 25‑pound weight loss.

The Trump‑Vance administration is using the same ‘flight‑risk’ argument that kept student protester Mahmoud Khalil and writer Rümeysa Öztürk in detention, framing Ovadia’s anti‑Israel protests as a security threat while launching a nationwide anti‑hate tour.

The piece links this case to broader concerns about Trump‑aligned advisers in a pro‑Russia Balkan enclave and ongoing illegal actions against Iran, highlighting a pattern of authoritarian enforcement.

items.subject: What’s the Matter With France?
bullets: French 5‑year CDS spreads have spiked, implying a 1.2% five‑year default probability, as markets fear France’s unsustainable debt, large deficits and an aging population driving pension costs
France’s statutory retirement age remains at 62‑9 months, far lower than peers, and political deadlock—Le Pen promising to roll it back—feeds fiscal strain and student protests
A French crisis could trigger a euro‑zone contagion; unlike the 2010s, a bailout faces German opposition and may be politically untenable despite the ECB’s “whatever it takes” pledge

items.subject: BOMBSHELL: Leaked Kimberly Guilfoyle Texts Reveal Brazen Corruption
bullets: The Wall Street Journal reported leaked private texts showing Kimberly Guilfoyle asked a Trump donor for $100,000 to cover her American Express bill, indicating personal financial ties to donors.
Guilfoyle’s messages repeatedly warned the donor to avoid creating a paper trail, suggesting awareness of illicit intent behind the cash request.

items.subject: Dems’ One Big Midterm Weakness Isn’t Looking So Bad Anymore
bullets: House Majority PAC raised a record $230 million in Q3 2026, its biggest quarter ever, while Senate Majority PAC pulled in a historic $202 million, signaling a sharp Democratic cash surge.
Democratic operatives say the influx of funds reflects brighter midterm prospects, eroding the Republicans’ perceived cash advantage that had been a key anxiety point.

items.subject: How Did October 7 Happen? Mehdi Asks a Former Israeli Intelligence Official
bullets: Former Israeli intelligence officer Avi Melamed says Prime Minister Netanyahu received multiple warnings—including a UAE president alert ten days before Oct. 7—and dismissed them, contributing to Israel’s unpreparedness for Hamas’s attack that killed over 1,000 and abducted 250+ people.

Melamed argues that Israeli military and intelligence downplayed a detailed Hamas battle plan obtained a year earlier, and Netanyahu has refused an internal investigation, framing the Gaza war as an operational failure.

The interview, available as a 52‑minute video for paid subscribers, also probes whether Israel’s actions in Gaza constitute genocide and critiques commentary from figures like Hillary Clinton and Charlie Kirk.

items.subject: Ex-CIA Officer Reacts to Insane Spy Scandal Rocking the Intelligence World
bullets: Michael Weiss and ex‑CIA officer Marc Polymeropoulos detail a spy scandal linking Germany’s former intelligence chief to an alleged Iranian plot to target U.S. bombers stationed in Britain.
They also examine bizarre inquiries about Kimberly Guilfoyle’s activities in Greece and allege Russian operatives left a gruesome calling card in politicians’ homes.

items.subject: Susan Collins Is the Living Worst
bullets: Collins faces a coin‑flip re‑election in Maine after voting to advance Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill,” which she claims enabled a $50 billion rural health‑care fund but added $3 billion to the state’s costs and cut SNAP and heating benefits.
The author labels Collins the “living worst” Republican, accusing her of enabling Trump’s agenda while only offering symbolic protest votes that are pre‑arranged to be ineffective.

items.subject: October 7 Three Years On: For Israel, a Day of Questions Must Also Ask the Difficult Kind
bullets: Three years after Hamas’s Oct. 7 attack, Israel is gearing up for its first post‑war election amid fresh claims that UAE and Egyptian officials warned it of the assault, raising doubts about the coalition’s narrative of surprise and its hard‑line rhetoric.

South African lawyers—including Blinne Ní Ghrálaigh and Adila Hassim—presented a genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice, alleging systematic crimes in Gaza and highlighting the conflict’s legal and moral dimensions.

The essay argues that public discourse still asks the wrong questions about the war, urging deeper scrutiny of Israel’s policies and the broader regional complicity in the ongoing humanitarian crisis.

items.subject: Donald Trump Is Buying Votes at $500 a Pop
bullets: Trump’s administration is sending $500 checks to about one million HealthCare.gov users and $90 checks to roughly 20 million Medicare Part B seniors and disabled people, claiming the payments are refunds for overcharges.

The $500 checks are marketed as a “refund” for alleged overcharges, yet the author argues that the drug‑company deals Trump cites did not produce significant savings, suggesting the money is essentially a vote‑buy.

items.subject: We’re less than one month out from Election Day.
bullets: National Republicans have poured tens of millions into the North Carolina Senate race, making it one of the most expensive contests of the cycle, while Democrats aim to flip the seat for the first time since 2008.
Roy Cooper urges supporters to donate $5 or more now to build grassroots momentum before early voting begins in eight days, stressing that the outcome will determine the Senate majority.

items.newsletter: Here Be Dragons from Barbara F. Walter
items.subject: Billionaires Don’t Need to Capture the Whole Government
bullets: Billionaires act as “stationary bandits,” seeking only the parts of government that protect and enhance their wealth—such as lax antitrust enforcement, low capital‑gain taxes, lucrative contracts, and data privacy—while avoiding unrelated policy areas.

The U.S. political system amplifies this effect: studies of 1,800 policy fights show that wealthy interests almost always succeed, whereas ordinary citizens rarely influence law, thanks to powerful lobbying, campaign financing, and legal expertise.

When many such bandits pursue their own gains, a tragedy of the commons emerges: each fears losing out if they restrain themselves, leading to cumulative erosion of the government’s effectiveness and eventual public backlash.

items.newsletter: Bill Kristol & Andrew Egger - The Bulwark
items.subject: Reasons for Hope. Reasons for Alarm.
bullets: Trump aides James Blair and Chris LaCivita spent hundreds of thousands consulting for a pro‑Russian Bosnian government while also fundraising for Trump’s PAC, raising concerns about foreign influence and cronyism.

Democrats hold a 51.1% to 43.4% advantage in generic congressional polls per FiftyPlusOne, but fear donor caution could blunt a historic midterm surge that could flip the Senate to a 54‑seat majority and win key governorships.

items.subject: State of the Race With Less Than 30 Days to Go.
bullets: Nate Silver’s updated model now gives Democrats a 93% chance of winning the House, projecting a 23‑seat gain over the current balance.

items.subject: 😳 GOP Panics That Racism and Trump’s Election-Rigging Attempts Will Fuel Democratic Victories
bullets: Republican insiders report panic as internal polls show the GOP could lose the House and possibly the Senate in November, driven by Trump’s unpopularity and a faltering economy.

GOP operatives warn that the Texas mid-decade gerrymander aimed at locking in Latino support backfired, with “dummymandered” districts likely delivering Democratic congressional wins due to voter backlash over economic hardship and anti‑Hispanic tactics.

items.subject: Top 8 questions about the “plague” situation
bullets: The YLE team rates the risk of a plague pandemic from the Russian lab worker’s death as a 1‑out of‑10 chance, citing virtually no chance of U.S. spread and no actionable steps for the public.
Pneumonic plague, if present, is contagious only with close contact and typically infects 1‑3 people per case; it is treatable with multiple antibiotics, though no U.S. vaccine exists since 1999.
CDC considers Yersinia pestis a potential bioweapon and maintains an under‑funded antibiotic stockpile, but there is currently no evidence the Russian case involved a engineered or weaponized strain.
